description: Internalized sexual stigma, identity conflict and hostility toward LGBTQ persons: evidence for and against the hypothesis discussed on 2026-08-29. Hypothesis (paraphrased from the German dialogue): conservative or heteronormative socialization, combined with a non-heterosexual orientation that contradicts the internalized norms, produces an inner conflict and psychological distress; the affected person then devalues or harms people who embody the unwanted part of the self, which may bring relief, protect self-esteem or restore group membership. The dialogue reformulated this as a largely unconscious chain (identity conflict -> threat to self-image and group membership -> shame and self-rejection -> stronger identification with the normative group -> demonstrative devaluation of LGBTQ persons -> temporary relief) and derived two testable predictions: the strength of the conflict between orientation and internalized norms should predict demonstrative devaluation, and the decisive predictor is homophobia combined with identity conflict rather than homophobia alone. Sourced findings are tagged 'measured value'; conjectures from the dialogue are tagged 'assumed value' with a confidence number. All DOIs were verified on 2026-08-29. Three sources were added beyond the dialogue (Adams 1996, MacInnis 2013, Weinstein 2012) because they test the popular attraction-based account directly.

sexual stigma influences internalized sexual stigma
triples.description: perceived level of societal repression against homosexuals predicted internalized homophobia and sex guilt in 86 gay men (Rowen 2002).

triples.name: internalized sexual stigma influences psychological distress
triples.description: internalized homophobia correlated with lower self-esteem, lower self-concept of emotional stability and higher sex guilt (Rowen 2002); internalized sexual stigma is linked to low self-esteem, depression, shame and feelings of rejection (Padilla 2025).

triples.name: internalized sexual stigma influences sex guilt
conservative values influences homophobia
triples.description: in Warriner 2013 fundamentalism, authoritarianism and sexism correlated with homophobia in lesbians but not in gay men; in gay men fundamentalism and authoritarianism correlated only with transphobia; correlates of internalized homophobia differed from those of homophobia. Gay and lesbian students scored lower than heterosexuals on homophobia, transphobia and fundamentalism.

triples.name: homophobia influences anti-gay aggression
triples.description: self-identified heterosexual men classified as homophobic reported more negative affect, anxiety and anger after a homosexual erotic video and gave more shocks to a supposedly homosexual opponent, but not to a heterosexual opponent (Bernat 2001).

triples.name: homosexual erotic stimulus influences anti-gay aggression
male role norms influences anti-gay aggression
triples.description: adherence to male role norms, especially antifemininity, was related to anger and aggression toward gay men via sexual prejudice and masculine gender role stress; interpreted as gender role enforcement (Parrott 2009).

triples.name: homophobia mediation male role norms
triples.description: sexual prejudice acts as mediator between male role norms and aggression toward gay men (Parrott 2009).

triples.name: gender role enforcement influences anti-gay aggression
self-esteem threat influences outgroup derogation
triples.description: White participants expressed more prejudice after negative feedback from a White evaluator; Black participants did so only after feedback from a Black evaluator, i.e. when the criticism could not be discounted as prejudice (Shapiro 2010). Derogation works as an esteem-protective strategy only when the threat is credible.

triples.name: intragroup aggression influences ingroup derogation
triples.description: computational model plus four behavioural studies: ingroup derogation evolves when intragroup conflict is lethal often enough, and it is stronger when participants feel vulnerable to aggression or see aggression cues (Wu 2016). General mechanism, not specific to sexual minorities.

triples.name: parental autonomy support influences implicit-explicit discrepancy
triples.description: low perceived parental autonomy support was associated with larger discrepancies between self-reported and implicit sexual orientation; the discrepancy was most pronounced when fathers were both low in autonomy support and homophobic (Weinstein 2012, four studies).

triples.name: implicit-explicit discrepancy influences homophobia
triples.description: the interaction of implicit-explicit discrepancy and low parental autonomy support predicted anti-gay responding indicative of reaction formation (Weinstein 2012). This is the closest published test of the dialogue's chain: norm-enforcing upbringing plus an orientation that contradicts the norm.

triples.name: homophobia influences genital arousal
triples.description: only the homophobic group of exclusively heterosexual men showed increased penile response to male homosexual video (Adams 1996); the authors could not distinguish arousal from anxiety, and the result is the origin of the popular attraction-based account.

triples.name: repressed same-sex attraction influences homophobia
triples.description: the attraction-based account. Tested with an implicit attraction measure in men and women: no evidence found; where relations existed, implicit same-sex attraction went with more positive evaluations of gay men and lesbians (MacInnis 2013). The dialogue rated this popular claim as hardly provable.

triples.name: heteronormative socialization influences identity conflict
triples.description: step 1 of the dialogue's chain: a strongly norm-oriented environment intensifies the conflict for a person whose orientation contradicts the norm; supported indirectly by Rowen 2002 (perceived repression) and Weinstein 2012 (autonomy-thwarting, homophobic fathers).

triples.name: identity conflict influences self-esteem threat
triples.description: step 2: the conflict threatens self-image and group membership.

triples.name: identity conflict influences psychological distress
triples.description: step 3: shame, guilt, fear and self-rejection; well supported at the level of internalized sexual stigma (Rowen 2002, Padilla 2025).

triples.name: identity conflict influences normative group identification
triples.description: step 4: stronger identification with the normative group as a way to secure belonging.

triples.name: normative group identification influences demonstrative devaluation
triples.description: step 5: devaluation of those who embody the unwanted trait, done visibly to prove membership; conjecture combining Shapiro 2010 and Wu 2016 with the sexual-minority case.

triples.name: identity conflict influences demonstrative devaluation
triples.description: prediction 1 of the dialogue: the stronger the conflict between orientation and internalized heteronormative values, the stronger, under certain conditions, the demonstrative devaluation of LGBTQ persons. Not yet tested as a complete path.

triples.name: demonstrative devaluation influences psychological relief
triples.description: step 6: temporary relief; the original formulation 'harming others makes one's own suffering feel smaller'. No study found that measures this pay-off in sexual-minority persons.

triples.name: demonstrative devaluation is a conscious strategy
triples.description: the original phrasing of the hypothesis implied a deliberate calculation; the dialogue judged an unconscious process to be more likely.

triples.name: demonstrative devaluation is a unconscious process
homophobia and identity conflict
triples.description: prediction 2 of the dialogue: the decisive predictor of demonstrative devaluation is the combination of homophobia and identity conflict, not homophobia alone.

triples.name: homophobia and identity conflict influences demonstrative devaluation
